newsitem.title: GERMANY: France and Germany agree proposals on EU reform.
newsitem.headline: France and Germany agree proposals on EU reform.

text.p: France and Germany said on Monday they had agreed on joint proposals to reform the European Union in a drive to boost the bloc's common foreign and security policy and streamline decision-making.

The German and French foreign ministers, Klaus Kinkel and Herve de Charette, said after talks in Bonn they would present their suggestions next Monday to the intergovernmental conference (IGC) discussing plans for a revised EU treaty.
Kinkel hailed the proposals as a major step forward. "We have made significant progress in the field of a common foreign and security policy," he told a joint news conference.

He said Paris and Bonn had agreed the Western European Union (WEU), the EU's fledgling defence arm, should be integrated in several phases into the bloc itself and that this should be stated in the new EU treaty.

The IGC should also agree to grant the European Council of EU leaders the power to issue guidelines on the work of the WEU. Humanitarian and peacekeeping military missions should also be enshrined in the new EU treaty, the ministers said.
They also said they had agreed on the need for a secretary-general to coordinate the common foreign and security policy and this would also form part of their proposals.
"For common foreign and security policy, the EU needs better co-ordination and preparation," Kinkel said.

Neither Kinkel nor de Charette went into detail on the issue, on which Bonn and Paris have not seen eye to eye in the past. France favoured a high-profile "Mr Europe" while Germany was reported to prefer a less visible bureaucrat.
As the EU prepares to invite more countries to join its ranks, the ministers also emphasised their desire to streamline decision-making by adopting more qualified majority voting.

"We can see the difficulties we have now and we can well imagine those we will have in the future if we do not undertake reform," said de Charette, who also underscored the countries' commitment to European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"You must not doubt the determination of both governments to apply what we have decided," he said.

When the decision is made on the initial EMU participants in early 1998, France and Germany will have met the necessary economic criteria and they will be ready to start the currency union on schedule in 1999, de Charette stressed.
The ministers also wanted to see a reform of the European Commission, the EU's executive body.

They said it should receive more responsibility but should contain fewer commissioners than the total number of EU member states. The powers of the commission president should also be strengthened, they said.
